comments.name: Boof
comments.body: With respect to the Presidency, the Founders's failure to anticipate the rise of political parties is an often overlooked flaw.  Specifically, the two major political parties now have too much influence over how their candidates are chosen.  The Presidential primary election process is woefully anachronistic and undemocratic at its core.  Just as two examples:  Why should a. few small states whose populations do not mirror the nation's diversity decide who survives to have a realistic chance?  And only a very small fraction of voters decide the two parties nominees (in 2024, 31 million voted in GOP & Dem primaries while more than 150M did in the general election).  The nomination process often produces a choice between 2 unqualified candidates in nation of 340M people.  The way we elect presidents is fundamentally flawed and it is the main reason it could produce someone like Trump.

But these initial major changes spread through nearly 15 years, and then, over more than 50 years, I hardly experienced any further TV viewing changes as I moved on my own, to different cities, but continually had access to comparable basic packages covering the range of Canadian (English, French, eventually some multicultural and Native language) and the standard US networks channels. Throughout, there were just fairly modest price increases, then even a Government decreed basic package at $25.CAD/month that I used to its very end until digital cable ended that option. 

But now, as I check out the alternatives and hear of others' experience, I am amazed at the loss of stability, predictability and user control of the ever more fragmented and expensive viewing. I doubt that the expanded choice is worth the added hassles and costs.

Icing almost certainly played a role, but another factor may have come into play.  There are some indications that the plane exceeded its critical Mach number early in the sequence of events, and entered a steep dive where the aircraft was literally uncontrollable.  This could be due to "Mach tuck".

In Mach tuck the plane is moving so fast that the center of lift over the wings moves to the rear causing the plane to pitch down and the tailplane no longer has any controlling effect.  Once this happens, the pilot may not be able to recover control, particularly if he didn't recognize it.  Also the aircraft may have experienced damage before the dive or during the dive which made recovery impossible.

Three parts of my experience could be of great help to those close to dying.  
•	A tremendous sense of well-being. I felt a renewed appreciation for being alive, a sense of peace, and lifting of the anxieties and depressing aspects that accompany aging.
•	An enhanced spiritual connection.  My experiences of connectedness and transcendence were profoundly meaningful.
•	An openness to death, loss, and grief. The most consequential of all was the ability to contemplate my own mortality without being overwhelmed 
It has profoundly changed my experience of living.
I am personally convinced it would not only be helpful to people who are dying but also help people make the most of the life that is left.

Like Yoga, pilates is free and costs nothing. You don't need classes or machines at all. Tons of videos online. Been doing mat pilates since 2005, picked it up from Mary Windsor and Pilates for Dummies videos. 

But, it's not for everybody. No one who I knew took it up. They all have their anodyne aches and pains now, and attribute them to "aging," to which, I mutter under my breath, "idiot".

Their punishment will only continue if they choose to enroll now. Pilates, properly done to the unconditioned, should make your discomfort rise to the verge of throwing up... that should pass if you stick with it, after a couple weeks. If it doesn't, you might need to stick to less intensive exercise until you can handle its demands, by way of losing weight and increasing muscular control, if possible. 

Remember, 20% of folx are exercise non-responders. If you suspect that is you, you are  probably right... and need to find another less intensive path.

comments.name: Max D
comments.body:
On the question of rudeness, I would focus more on your impact on other people rather than merely being in public. Parks, plazas, and university campuses are all examples of spaces that can both be public but also often at times don't have people around to potentially bother. 

So why is loud noise rude if it impacts others? Arthur Schopenhauer puts it well in his essay "On Noise": noise "is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought." You cannot always know what's going on in someone else's head, but there's a good chance in a random place full of people that someone is thinking about something important. Or rather, they were thinking about something important until you started blasting shorts videos on full audio. 

There is also the simple medical fact that noise pollution harms people. Most people are aware of the health effects of second hand smoking, but studies show that second hand noise causes a large range of medical issues from higher stress to hearing loss. 

If noise prevents people from thinking about important things while also giving them physical harm, are there times when it's ok to be noisy? Probably, but perhaps you should start by asking the people around you if they're ok with you being loud first.

As a former forensic anthropology student, with two postgrad degrees in archaeology: I disagree with the interpretations.

The blow is from above, the penetration is 1/2" round through the thin scapula. 

I disagree that this is a kill shot from the front. It's from the back.  1/2" is too big for an arrow but not large enough for a strong spear.  

More likely to be accidental than intentional. Fell on something (like a sharpened stake). Such a stake could be part of the windbreak fence or one of many in a pit for catching game. Or, it could be the game: got gored by a deer or elk antler, which fits with the blow from above.

Yes, it could be interpersonal violence. I just don't think the placement or size of the wound is a slam dunk for a kill shot. The best kill shot is in the heart, but hearts are hard to get at from the front or back because of the ribcage. Wounding in the gut will do the job, and it's soft and easy. If you're lucky and really close, you can shove up from the gut into the heart and lungs under the ribcage.

Or it could be both: poor dude was out hunting and someone else accidentally got him in the back...but again the 1/2" size is odd for that scenario.

We’re going to have to make major changes, not that I’ve seen any political candidate this Election Day ever say that.
I’ve long asked The Times to make sustainability a major theme, including its implications for many conventional issues, what’s being done around the world to address it, and whether it’s working.
Business as usual, for journalism, other sectors, the way other issues are conventionally seen, how our economies run, how we live—only takes us so far.

comments.name: Alex Tamayo
comments.body: The syncretic rituals in Metlatónoc still reflect what Día de los Muertos once meant for Mexico's rural and urban poor. The wonderful pictures that accompany this article have an almost anthropological value. They are snapshots of a vanishing tradition that is still alive only in the most remote parts of Mexico. Ever since Madonna declared her fascination with Frida Kahlo and a James Bond movie choreographed a fake Day of the Dead parade filmed in Mexico City’s Zócalo, urban Mexicans have adopted this Halloween-like style and advertise it to the world as a bona fide “Mexican” celebration of the dead. The remoteness of places like Metlatónoc in Guerrero state has kept them from turning Day of the Dead rituals into a Halloween party. There are other reasons why people from these regions have a very intimate relationship with their dead: extreme poverty, lack of health services, and the violence of the cartels that target the civilian population and control the whole region make death a constant and imminent presence in their lives.

​Growing up in the Gravesend Houses in Coney Island, Brooklyn, it certainly wasn't paradise, but it offered a laid-back environment with Kaiser Park right across the way and beautiful views out over the bay.

​My late mentor, Horton Shaw—long before our days together at New York City Transit—used to talk about how back in the Governor Thomas E. Dewey era, they actually conducted aerial surveys when planning these complexes to ensure proper layout, light, and access to good community amenities. Unfortunately, all of that shifted in the 1970s with a steep decline in maintenance, a loss of respect for the properties, and the devastating impact of the drug epidemic.

​While a few places managed to preserve their quality of life, NYCHA is largely looking to exit the property management business today—and given the history, it is hard to blame them. He is, quite simply, a Russian revanchist. And anything that keeps him from achieving his revanchist agenda is a security treat. That, in turn, means no independent, liberal democratic states along Russia’s borders. Those states are by Putin’s definition a threat to Russia’s – but really his – existence. 

Moreover, if Putin takes Ukraine it won't be ruled the way White Russia is now. Putin will crush Ukrainian culture, just like his czarist and Soviet forebearers tried to do for centuries, because cultural genocide has always been Russia's goal for Ukraine.

Blaming the U.S. for Putin's aggression requires that you ignore all this. But it shouldn’t be ignored, or forgotten.

comments.name: Kathleen
comments.body: Heating costs must be considered. When my husband built his zone 7 greenhouse, he did three things to keep them low. First, the greenhouse is double insulated, with protection both outside and inside the frame. This gives three inches all around of trapped air, which is an excellent insulator, and also make sure there's a good 'seal.' Second, he built a 1000 gallon raised pond along the north wall. The water takes on heat during the day, and releases it at night. A small pump keeps the water moving. Third, he built a sand table along the south wall, with three heating cables to keep the damp sand warm. These three features mean he never has to supply additional heat - even when it gets down to -1 F outside - and they also mean he won't get divorced over heating bills!
